problems.title: Subsets
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums containing unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution must not contain duplicate subsets. The subsets can be returned in any order.
problems.understanding: For every element, we have two decisions: take or don't take. For n elements, there are 2^n possible subsets. Both naive binary decision-tree traversal and loop-based incremental backtracking generate all 2^n subsets.

naive.title: Naive Solution
naive.html: Generate every subset by recursively deciding whether to take or not take each element.

code.py:
class Solution:
    def subsets(self, nums):
        result = []

        def backtrack(index, current):
            if index == len(nums):
                result.append(current[:])
                return

            # Don't take nums[index]
            backtrack(index + 1, current)

            # Take nums[index]
            current.append(nums[index])
            backtrack(index + 1, current)
            current.pop()

        backtrack(0, [])
        return result

complexity: Aux Space: O(n) recursion + current path

problems.intuition: The standard optimized backtracking version builds subsets incrementally. At each level of recursion, append the current path to result, then try adding each remaining candidate starting from start index.
problems.approach:
1. Define backtrack(start, current).
  2. Every current state is a valid subset, so append a copy to result.
  3. Loop i from start to len(nums) - 1.
  4. Append nums[i] to current.
  5. Recurse with backtrack(i + 1, current).
  6. Pop nums[i] to backtrack.
problems.takeaway: Both have the same asymptotic complexity. The optimized version has a cleaner subset-generation pattern.

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.statement: Given candidates and target, find combinations whose sum equals target. Elements can be reused.
problems.understanding: Let T = target and k = len(candidates). The recursion depth can be approximately T when the smallest candidate is 1. We must avoid generating permutations of the same combination.

naive.title: Naive Solution
naive.html: Try every candidate at every step without pruning.
complexity: Output Space: depends on number of valid combinations

problems.intuition: Use start index to avoid generating the same combination in different orders, and sort candidates to break the loop early when a candidate exceeds the remaining target.
problems.approach:
1. Sort candidates array.
  2. Define backtrack(start, remaining, current).
  3. If remaining == 0, append current[:] to result and return.
  4. Iterate i from start to len(candidates) - 1.
  5. If candidates[i] > remaining, break early (pruning).
  6. Append candidate, call backtrack(i, remaining - num, current) (pass i to allow reuse), and pop.

optimal.title: Code (Optimized)
complexity: Output Space: O(number of combinations × T)

problems.takeaway: The important optimization is avoiding permutations of the same combination and pruning candidates larger than the remaining target.

problems.title: Permutations
problems.understanding: Drawing tokens in different orders creates distinct permutations (n! arrangements). At each level, choose an unused element.

naive.title: Naive Solution
naive.html: At every level, scan the entire array and choose an unused element using if num in current, which costs O(n) per check.

problems.intuition: Use a boolean used[] array to keep track of used elements in O(1) time instead of checking membership in current path.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize used = [False] * len(nums).
  2. Define backtrack(current).
  3. If len(current) == len(nums), append copy to result.
  4. Loop i from 0 to len(nums) - 1. If used[i], skip.
  5. Set used[i] = True, append nums[i], recurse, pop, and set used[i] = False.
problems.takeaway: Although the asymptotic time remains O(n × n!), the optimized solution removes the repeated O(n) membership search.

problems.title: Subsets II
problems.statement: Array may contain duplicates. We need unique subsets.
problems.understanding: When input elements contain duplicates, standard subset branching generates identical subsets multiple times.

naive.title: Naive Solution
naive.html: Generate all 2^n subsets and put them into a set to eliminate duplicate subsets.

code.py:
class Solution:
    def subsetsWithDup(self, nums):
        nums.sort()
        result = set()

        def backtrack(index, current):
            if index == len(nums):
                result.add(tuple(current))
                return

            # Don't take
            backtrack(index + 1, current)

            # Take
            current.append(nums[index])
            backtrack(index + 1, current)
            current.pop()

        backtrack(0, [])
        return [list(x) for x in result]

problems.intuition: Sort the array and skip duplicate choices at the same recursion level.
problems.approach:
1. Sort nums.
  2. Define backtrack(start, current) and append current[:].
  3. Loop i from start to len(nums) - 1.
  4. If i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1], continue.
  5. Append nums[i], call backtrack(i + 1, current), and pop.
problems.takeaway:
Critical Pattern: if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]: continue
Skip duplicates at the same recursion level, but allow duplicates at different levels.

problems.title: Combination Sum II
problems.statement: Each candidate can be used only once, and candidates may contain duplicates. Find unique combinations summing to target.
problems.understanding: Combines single-use constraint with duplicate candidate values. We cannot reuse an element (use i + 1) and must prune duplicate sibling choices.

naive.title: Naive Solution
naive.html: Generate combinations recursively and use a set to remove duplicates.

code.py:
class Solution:
    def combinationSum2(self, candidates, target):
        result = set()
        candidates.sort()

        def backtrack(index, remaining, current):
            if remaining == 0:
                result.add(tuple(current))
                return

            if index == len(candidates) or remaining < 0:
                return

            # Don't choose
            backtrack(index + 1, remaining, current)

            # Choose
            current.append(candidates[index])
            backtrack(
                index + 1,
                remaining - candidates[index],
                current
            )
            current.pop()

        backtrack(0, target, [])
        return [list(x) for x in result]

problems.intuition: Sort array, skip duplicate choices at the same level (i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i - 1]), and prune when candidates[i] > remaining.
problems.approach:
1. Sort candidates.
  2. Define backtrack(start, remaining, current).
  3. If remaining == 0, append copy to result.
  4. Loop i from start to len(candidates) - 1.
  5. Skip duplicates at same level: if i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i - 1]: continue.
  6. Break if candidates[i] > remaining.
  7. Recurse with i + 1 because each element can be used once.

optimal.title: Code (Optimized)
complexity: Output Space: O(number of valid combinations × n)

problems.takeaway:
Important Difference:
Combination Sum uses backtrack(i, ...) (can reuse the same element).
Combination Sum II uses backtrack(i + 1, ...) (cannot reuse it).

problems.title: Word Search
problems.statement: Find whether a word exists in a grid by moving up/down/left/right.
problems.understanding: Let R = rows, C = columns, L = word length. The first character can start from R × C cells. After that, there are up to 4 choices initially and at most 3 choices afterward because we don't immediately revisit the previous cell.

naive.title: Naive Solution
naive.html: Try every cell as the starting position and recursively explore all four directions.

problems.intuition: Prune impossible searches before DFS: check whether the word's character frequency exists in the board, search from the rarer end of the word (reverse if board_count[word[0]] > board_count[word[-1]]), and use in-place marking.
problems.approach:
1. Count character frequencies in board and word using Counter.
  2. If board lacks any character required by word, return False.
  3. If board_count[word[0]] > board_count[word[-1]], reverse word to start search from the rarer end.
  4. Run DFS from matching start cells using in-place '#' cell marking and backtracking.
problems.takeaway: The optimization mainly improves practical pruning (character counting & rarer-end search), rather than changing the worst-case exponential bound.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning
problems.statement: Partition a string such that every substring is a palindrome. Example for "aab": ["a", "a", "b"], ["aa", "b"].
problems.understanding: There can be exponentially many partitions. Checking substring palindromes on the fly adds repeated O(n) work.

naive.title: Naive Solution
naive.html: At every position, try every possible substring and check whether it is a palindrome with string == string[::-1].

problems.intuition: Precompute whether every substring is a palindrome using 2D Dynamic Programming in O(n^2) time before backtracking.
problems.approach:
1. Build 2D boolean array palindrome[n][n].
  2. Set single characters palindrome[i][i] = True.
  3. Fill DP table for lengths 2 to n: palindrome[left][right] = True if characters match and inner substring is palindrome.
  4. Backtrack from start = 0, using palindrome[start][end] for O(1) checks.

optimal.title: Code (Optimized)
complexity: Aux Space: O(n^2) DP + O(n) recursion

problems.takeaway: Precompute expensive repeated checks → Backtracking becomes cleaner and faster.

problems.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
problems.statement: Given digits 2–9, generate all possible letter combinations. Example for "23": ad, ae, af, bd, be, bf, cd, ce, cf.
problems.understanding: Each digit gives at most 4 choices. For n digits, total combinations is O(4^n).

naive.title: Naive Solution
naive.html: Build all combinations using recursion with a dictionary lookup for key mapping.

problems.intuition: Use a list of mappings and construct the string directly with index offsets (ord(digits[index]) - ord('0')).
problems.approach:
1. Return [] if digits is empty.
  2. Initialize array phone indexed from 0 to 9.
  3. Define backtrack(index, current).
  4. If index == len(digits), append "".join(current) to result.
  5. Get mapped string using phone[ord(digits[index]) - ord('0')].
  6. Loop through characters, append, recurse index + 1, and pop.

code.py:
class Solution:
    def letterCombinations(self, digits):
        if not digits:
            return []

        phone = [
            "",
            "",
            "abc",
            "def",
            "ghi",
            "jkl",
            "mno",
            "pqrs",
            "tuv",
            "wxyz"
        ]

        result = []

        def backtrack(index, current):
            if index == len(digits):
                result.append("".join(current))
                return

            letters = phone[ord(digits[index]) - ord('0')]

            for char in letters:
                current.append(char)
                backtrack(index + 1, current)
                current.pop()

        backtrack(0, [])
        return result

problems.takeaway: Again, the asymptotic complexity doesn't change much; the optimization is primarily cleaner/faster implementation.

problems.title: N-Queens
problems.statement: Place n queens on an n × n board so that no two queens attack each other.
problems.understanding: At each row, we have up to n choices. Placements must be checked for column, positive diagonal (row + col), and negative diagonal (row - col) collisions.

naive.title: Naive Solution
naive.html: Try placing a queen in every column of every row, then check whether the board is valid with an is_safe helper function scanning the board in O(n) time.
complexity: Aux Space: O(n^2) board + O(n) recursion
Output Space: O(number of solutions × n^2)

problems.intuition: Instead of scanning the board every time, maintain three sets: columns, positive diagonals (row + col), and negative diagonals (row - col). Then checking whether a position is safe becomes O(1).
problems.approach:
1. Initialize board and three hash sets: columns, positive_diagonals, negative_diagonals.
  2. Define backtrack(row). If row == n, add formatted board to result.
  3. Loop col from 0 to n - 1.
  4. If col in columns, row + col in positive_diagonals, or row - col in negative_diagonals, skip.
  5. Place "Q", add to all 3 sets, recurse row + 1, and then backtrack (remove "Q" and remove from sets).

optimal.title: Code (Optimized)

code.py:
class Solution:
    def solveNQueens(self, n):
        result = []

        board = [["."] * n for _ in range(n)]

        columns = set()
        positive_diagonals = set()  # row + col
        negative_diagonals = set()  # row - col

        def backtrack(row):
            if row == n:
                result.append(
                    ["".join(r) for r in board]
                )
                return

            for col in range(n):
                if col in columns:
                    continue

                if row + col in positive_diagonals:
                    continue

                if row - col in negative_diagonals:
                    continue

                # Place queen
                board[row][col] = "Q"
                columns.add(col)
                positive_diagonals.add(row + col)
                negative_diagonals.add(row - col)

                backtrack(row + 1)

                # Backtrack
                board[row][col] = "."
                columns.remove(col)
                positive_diagonals.remove(row + col)
                negative_diagonals.remove(row - col)

        backtrack(0)

        return result

complexity: Aux Space: O(n^2) board + O(n) sets/recursion
Output Space: O(number of solutions × n^2)

problems.takeaway: Safety check is reduced to O(1) using sets for columns and diagonals. The search itself remains exponential (O(n × n!) approx).
